title: Power BI's Four Views and the Load vs Transform Decision
learning_objective: Identify the purpose of the Report, Table, Model, and Power Query editor views, and explain why Transform Data should be chosen over Load when a file's column types have not yet been checked.
description_for_ai: Power BI Desktop has three main-window views reached from icons on the far-left edge: Report view (the default blank canvas where charts are built), Table view (one table at a time, as rows and columns, used to check what a number actually is when a visual looks wrong), and Model view (boxes and lines showing how tables relate). The Power Query editor is a separate window, not a tab, that opens only when Transform Data is clicked; it has its own ribbon and its own taskbar entry, so a trainee who 'loses' Power BI mid-session has usually just lost track of this second window. When importing a file (Home, Get Data, Text/CSV), the preview offers Load and Transform Data. Load commits the file exactly as Power BI has guessed its column types, and Power BI infers types by sampling roughly the first couple of hundred rows, so a fault further down the file is missed at the exact moment it matters. Transform Data opens Power Query first and commits nothing, which is the correct default any time column types have not yet been verified, independent of whether the file is already known to be dirty.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Treating the Power Query editor as a lost or crashed window instead of checking the taskbar for its separate entry. Clicking Load on a first import because the preview looks clean, without having checked column types. Believing Report view is where data cleaning happens, when it is Table view and the Power Query editor that serve that purpose. Assuming Power BI's automatic type inference reads the whole file rather than a sample of early rows.
example_code_for_ai:
# Not code - a Power BI Desktop workflow.
# Home ribbon -> Get Data -> Text/CSV -> select file
# Preview dialog shows two buttons: [Load] [Transform Data]
# Choosing Transform Data opens the separate Power Query editor window
# before anything is committed to the model.

title: Setting Correct Data Types After Loading
learning_objective: Set the correct data type for a promoted-header column in Power Query, and explain why an identifier column such as RiderID must be typed as Text rather than a number.
description_for_ai: After Get Data, the Power Query editor's column headers should be checked first: if columns read Column1, Column2 instead of real names, the header row was not promoted, fixed via Home, Use First Row as Headers. Each column then gets an explicit type via the column header's type icon: date-shaped columns to Date, identifier columns (any ID field, e.g. RiderID, RouteID, CustomerID, DeliveryID) to Text, count-like whole numbers to Whole Number, and currency-like decimals to Fixed Decimal Number. The test for whether an ID column should be Text is whether arithmetic on it means anything: rider fourteen plus rider twenty-two is not rider thirty-six, so an ID column typed as a number is wrong even though it looks numeric. Typing an ID column as a number causes two silent problems: Power BI may auto-sum it the instant it lands in a visual, and leading zeros are stripped, so an ID like 007 silently becomes 7, which then fails to match the same ID stored as text in another table, breaking a relationship with no visible error.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Leaving an identifier column as Whole Number because the values look numeric, instead of applying the arithmetic-meaning test. Not noticing Column1/Column2-style headers, meaning the promote-headers step was skipped. Typing a currency field as a plain Decimal Number rather than Fixed Decimal Number, which allows rounding to drift a total. Assuming a type set once in Power Query cannot silently revert - a later step can change a type back without warning.
not_yet_taught: trimming whitespace and filtering as a rule

title: Trimming Whitespace, Filtering as a Rule, and Reading Applied Steps
learning_objective: Apply Trim to remove invisible leading or trailing spaces on key columns, write a filter as a reusable rule rather than an edit tied to specific row numbers, and read the Applied Steps pane as an ordered, reorderable record of every transformation.
description_for_ai: A trailing or leading space on a key column (e.g. 'R-014 ' versus 'R-014') is invisible on screen but makes the two values different strings to the computer, so a relationship built on that key produces blanks with nothing turning red. The fix is Transform, Format, Trim, applied to every key column that will be used in a relationship. When removing bad rows, the correct approach is to write a filter as a condition true of any file with the same shape, such as 'remove rows where CustomerID is blank', rather than an edit describing this one file, such as 'delete rows 41,281 to 41,283' - the rule-based filter still works correctly next month, while the row-number edit will quietly delete three different, innocent rows once the file changes. The Applied Steps pane, on the right of the Power Query editor, lists every transformation in order (Source, Promoted Headers, Changed Type, Trimmed Text, Filtered Rows, etc.); each step can be clicked to see the table exactly as it stood at that point, and steps can be dragged to reorder them, which matters because a step run in the wrong order (e.g. filtering before types are set) can behave differently than intended.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Deleting bad rows by row number or by manually scrolling and removing them, instead of writing a condition-based filter. Assuming Trim did nothing because no visible change appears on screen - Trim's effect is confirmed by checking the Applied Steps pane for a Trimmed Text step, not by looking at the data. Not noticing that reordering a step (for example moving a filter above a type-change step) changes the result. Treating the Applied Steps pane as a static log rather than an editable, reorderable sequence.

title: Table Grain and the Flat-Table Trap
learning_objective: Explain what a table's grain is, predict why counting a name column in a flat, pre-merged table produces a wrong count, and state which real-world entity that count is actually measuring.
description_for_ai: The grain of a table is what one row represents. When five related tables (a delivery fact table plus rider, route, customer, and date details) are pre-merged into one flat table before import, the grain becomes one row per delivery, not one row per rider - so a rider's name is repeated once for every delivery that rider made. Counting that name column therefore does not count riders, it counts delivery-rows that happen to have that name attached; with 68 real riders and 41,280 deliveries, a Count on RiderName in the flat table returns 41,280, not 68, with no error or warning because the calculation is arithmetically correct for what the table actually contains. The lesson generalises: before trusting any count or sum, first ask what one row of the table represents, because a plausible, error-free number can still be a completely wrong answer to the question that was asked.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Assuming a large, precise-looking number is correct because it produced no error. Believing repeated values in a merged/flat table indicate corrupt or duplicated data, rather than recognising that grain has changed to one-row-per-event. Using Count instead of Count Distinct on a flat table without first checking what the table's grain actually is - though the deeper fix is not to flatten the tables in the first place. Confusing 'the rider appears many times' with 'the data is wrong' instead of 'the table answers questions about deliveries, not riders'.
not_yet_taught: fact vs dimension classification and relationships

title: Classifying Fact vs Dimension Tables and Building Relationships
learning_objective: Classify a table as fact or dimension using the filter-or-group-by versus sum-or-count rule of thumb, draw a one-to-many relationship in Model view, and read the cardinality Power BI infers.
description_for_ai: A fact table records events, one row per thing that happened, and is long and narrow (e.g. swiftroute_deliveries, one row per delivery). A dimension table describes things, one row per thing that exists, and is short and wide (e.g. riders, routes, customers, dates). The practical rule of thumb: if you filter by it or group by it, it is a dimension; if you sum it or count it, it is a fact. A relationship is drawn in Model view by dragging the key field from a dimension (e.g. riders[RiderID]) onto the matching field in the fact table (swiftroute_deliveries[RiderID]); Power BI then infers and displays the cardinality, which should read one-to-many with the 'one' on the dimension side. If the dialogue ever reads many-to-many, that signals the dimension table has duplicate keys and needs investigating before the relationship is trusted. A date dimension additionally needs Table Tools, Mark as Date Table, selecting its date key column, before time-intelligence calculations will work correctly. Once relationships are built correctly, a filter applied on a dimension (e.g. clicking a hub on a riders slicer) travels from the 'one' side into the 'many' side, filtering the fact table.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Classifying a table as fact or dimension by its size or column count rather than by whether it is summed/counted (fact) or filtered/grouped by (dimension). Accepting a many-to-many cardinality without checking the dimension table for duplicate keys. Dragging the relationship in the wrong direction, or connecting the wrong pair of columns, so the join fails silently or matches on the wrong field. Forgetting to mark the date table, which silently breaks time-intelligence measures later without an error at the point the table was built.

title: Diagnosing Silent Relationship Failures and Choosing Cross-Filter Direction
learning_objective: Diagnose a relationship that builds without error but produces blanks as a trailing-space fault fixed upstream in Power Query, and explain why cross-filter direction should default to Single rather than Both.
description_for_ai: A relationship can build with no error and still be wrong: if a key column has a trailing space on one side (e.g. 'LAG-07 ' in one table versus 'LAG-07' in another), the two values look identical on screen but are different strings to Power BI, so the relationship produces blanks for every mismatched row while showing nothing red. The fix is upstream, in Power Query, Transform, Format, Trim, applied to the key column in both tables involved - never by editing the source file by hand and never by patching the model. Separately, every relationship has a cross-filter direction property, Single or Both. Both looks helpful because it lets filters travel back up out of the fact table into a different dimension, but this can make a completely unrelated chart elsewhere in the report change for reasons nobody can trace. The safe default is Single, changed to Both only for a specific, understood reason.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Trying to fix a trailing-space relationship failure inside the model instead of tracing it back to Power Query and applying Trim to the source column in both tables. Applying Trim to only one of the two tables' key columns, leaving the relationship still broken. Setting cross-filter direction to Both by default because it seems more flexible, without a specific reason. Assuming a relationship that 'builds successfully' (no dialog error) is automatically correct, rather than checking for blanks in a visual that uses it.

title: Writing Aggregation Measures with COUNTROWS and SUM
learning_objective: Write a named DAX measure using COUNTROWS to count rows in a fact table and SUM to total a numeric column, and explain why a named measure is preferred over dragging a raw field into a visual.
description_for_ai: A DAX measure is created via right-click on a table (commonly a dedicated hidden _Measures table), New Measure, and is given an explicit name rather than left as a dragged field. COUNTROWS(table) counts the rows of the specified table, e.g. Total Deliveries = COUNTROWS(swiftroute_deliveries). SUM(table[column]) totals a numeric column, e.g. Total Revenue = SUM(swiftroute_deliveries[DeliveryFee]). The value of naming a measure is not the arithmetic, which is trivial, but that every later measure in the model can refer to it by name in square brackets (e.g. [Total Deliveries]) - a capability a raw dragged field does not have. A measure automatically respects whatever filters are active in the visual or page it is placed on, recalculating per context rather than being fixed to one number.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Dragging a raw column into a visual and applying an aggregation (e.g. Sum) via the Fields well instead of writing a named measure, which cannot be referenced by other measures. Leaving a measure with Power BI's default generated name instead of a clear, purposeful name. Writing COUNTROWS against the wrong table (a dimension instead of the fact table), producing a count of dimension rows rather than events. Forgetting that a measure's result changes depending on the filter context of the visual it sits in - it is not a single fixed number.

title: Writing Ratio Measures with DIVIDE Instead of the Slash Operator
learning_objective: Write a ratio measure using DIVIDE, and explain what it returns for a zero-denominator case compared to the plain slash operator.
description_for_ai: DIVIDE(numerator, denominator) is DAX's safe division function, used in place of the plain slash operator whenever a measure might ever be evaluated with a zero or missing denominator - for example a rider who joined recently with zero deliveries so far. The plain slash operator returns an error or Infinity when the denominator is zero, which surfaces on the report viewer's screen, not the report author's. DIVIDE checks the denominator first and returns blank instead, which is the honest outcome: not zero, not an error, simply nothing to report. A typical usage combines a filtered CALCULATE with DIVIDE, e.g. On-Time Deliveries = CALCULATE([Total Deliveries], swiftroute_deliveries[Status] = "On time"), then On-Time Rate = DIVIDE([On-Time Deliveries], [Total Deliveries]).
common_mistakes_for_ai: Writing a ratio measure with the plain slash operator (a / b) instead of DIVIDE, risking a visible error or Infinity when filtered to a zero-denominator case. Assuming DIVIDE returns zero rather than blank when the denominator is zero - these are different outcomes with different meanings. Not testing a ratio measure against a low-volume or zero-volume filter before treating it as finished. Building the ratio's numerator with a plain equality filter instead of CALCULATE, so it does not actually respond to slicing.
not_yet_taught: CALCULATE and filter context in depth

title: Changing Filter Context with CALCULATE
learning_objective: Read a CALCULATE-based measure aloud in plain English and explain that it evaluates its base expression under the visual's existing filters plus whatever additional condition is supplied.
description_for_ai: CALCULATE(expression, condition) evaluates expression under the current filter context - whatever a visual, slicer, or page has already filtered to - with condition applied on top. A measure such as On-Time Deliveries = CALCULATE([Total Deliveries], swiftroute_deliveries[Status] = "On time") should be readable aloud as plain English: 'work out my delivery count, but first, on top of whatever the visual already filtered, also require the status to be On time.' Being able to narrate a CALCULATE measure this way is treated as the verification test itself: a measure that cannot be read aloud and explained cannot be verified, and should not be shipped. CALCULATE is the mechanism behind every filtered aggregation and every time-intelligence measure in DAX.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Treating CALCULATE's condition argument as replacing all existing filters rather than adding to them on top of the current filter context. Being unable to state in plain English what a CALCULATE measure does before using it in a report. Assuming CALCULATE always narrows results - it can also widen them, for example when used with a time-intelligence function that shifts the date filter rather than adding to it. Writing a filter condition directly as a boolean inside CALCULATE without checking it matches the column's actual stored values (e.g. exact casing and spelling of 'On time').

title: Time-Intelligence Measures with DATEADD and a Marked Date Table
learning_objective: Write a time-intelligence measure using CALCULATE and DATEADD to shift the date filter by one month, and explain why this only works correctly against a table marked as the model's date table.
description_for_ai: A time-intelligence measure combines CALCULATE with a date-shifting function such as DATEADD(dates[DateKey], -1, MONTH), which moves the active date filter back by the stated interval before re-evaluating the base measure: Deliveries Previous Month = CALCULATE([Total Deliveries], DATEADD(dates[DateKey], -1, MONTH)). This pattern depends entirely on the dates table having been marked as the model's official date table (Table Tools, Mark as Date Table) - without that step, DATEADD and similar functions do not shift correctly. A month with no prior-period data in the model (e.g. the first month present) correctly returns blank for its 'previous month' measure; this is expected behaviour, not a bug to be fixed. Combining a current-period measure with its shifted counterpart via DIVIDE produces a month-on-month change measure, e.g. Month on Month Change = DIVIDE([Total Deliveries] - [Deliveries Previous Month], [Deliveries Previous Month]).
common_mistakes_for_ai: Writing a DATEADD-based measure before marking the date table, so the calculation silently fails to shift periods correctly. Treating a blank result for the earliest period's 'previous month' as an error to be patched rather than the correct, expected outcome. Using the plain slash operator instead of DIVIDE inside a change-over-time measure, reintroducing the divide-by-zero risk. Confusing DATEADD's direction argument (positive moves forward, negative moves backward) and shifting the wrong way.

title: Verifying a DAX Measure Before Trusting It
learning_objective: Apply the predict, run, reconcile, and break verification workflow to a finished DAX measure before treating its output as trustworthy.
description_for_ai: Before trusting any DAX measure, four steps are applied in order: predict the expected value aloud based on business knowledge before running anything; run the measure and read its value at the unfiltered total level; reconcile that value against a completely different surface, such as manually filtering the fact table in Table view and reading the row count directly, to confirm the two independent paths agree; and finally break it deliberately, for example filtering the report to a single low-volume entity, to check the measure still behaves sensibly (no error, no nonsensical spike) under an edge-case filter. A measure that only agrees with expectations at the grand total but has never been reconciled against a second, independent calculation path or tested under an unusual filter has not actually been verified, even if its headline number looks right.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Treating a measure as verified because its total-level value matches expectation, without reconciling against an independent second calculation. Skipping the deliberate-break step, so a divide-by-zero or blank-handling problem is only discovered later, in front of the actual report audience. Reconciling against a number produced by the same measure or the same filter path, which is not independent verification. Predicting an expected value only after running the measure, which removes the ability to catch a genuinely wrong result that still looks plausible.

title: Designing a Dashboard Backwards from Audience and Decision
learning_objective: Sketch a dashboard layout starting from a named audience and the decision they need to make, placing the most important number where a reader's eye lands first.
description_for_ai: Dashboard design starts from a named audience and the decision they need to make, not from the fields that happen to be available in the model - a short paper sketch (title and filters across the top, KPI cards in a row, a ranked chart, a detail table) done before opening Power BI saves significant rebuilding time later. Readers scan a screen from the top left first, the same way they read a page of text, so the most important, decision-driving number should be placed where the eye lands first, not buried lower on the canvas or on a second page.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Starting a dashboard build by dragging in whatever fields exist, rather than first identifying who will read it and what decision it supports. Placing the least important visual (e.g. a decorative chart) in the top-left position, where the most important KPI should sit. Skipping the sketch step and treating layout as something to fix after every visual is already built. Designing a dashboard with no single primary audience in mind, producing a report that serves everyone only partially.
example_code_for_ai:
# Paper sketch, before opening Power BI:
# [ Title and filters across the top ]
# [ KPI card ] [ KPI card ] [ KPI card ] [ KPI card ]
# [ ranked bar chart, left ]      [ detail table, right ]
# Audience: Adaeze, Operations Lead. Decision: where to focus attention.
not_yet_taught: axis field and sort choice for ranked charts

title: Turning a Metric into a KPI with a Target
learning_objective: Attach a target value to a plain metric to turn it into a KPI, and explain what that target changes about how the number should be read.
description_for_ai: A plain metric (e.g. On-Time Rate at 82.0%) becomes a KPI once a target is attached to it (e.g. an SLA target of 90%), either via a card's target/goal setting or by switching to the dedicated KPI visual with Value, Trend axis, and Target fields set. The build order for a dashboard's headline numbers is cards first, before any chart, because the headline answers should exist before time is spent on a chart nobody has confirmed is needed yet. The difference a target makes is interpretive: 82.0% alone is simply a fact, while 82.0% against a 90% target is eight points below promise and demands a decision, which is the entire purpose of turning a metric into a KPI.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Building charts before the headline KPI cards exist, reversing the correct build order. Displaying a metric without any target or benchmark, leaving the reader to guess whether the number is good or bad. Setting a target that does not correspond to an actual agreed business SLA or goal. Treating the KPI visual as purely decorative rather than as the object that turns a number into a decision trigger.
example_code_for_ai:
# KPI visual configuration:
# Value = [On-Time Rate]
# Trend axis = dates[MonthName]
# Target = 90%
# Reading: "82.0% against a 90% target" carries different meaning than "82.0%" alone.
not_yet_taught: axis field and sort choice for ranked charts

title: Choosing the Right Axis Field and Sort Direction for a Ranked Chart
learning_objective: Choose a unique ID field rather than a duplicate-prone name field for a ranked chart's axis, and sort a horizontal bar chart in the direction that puts the worst performer where the reader will actually see it.
description_for_ai: When two entities share the same display name (e.g. two different routes both called 'Apapa to Ikeja', with distinct RouteIDs LAG-07 and APA-01), putting the name field on a chart's axis silently merges them into one averaged bar, hiding whichever of the two was the true worst performer. The fix is to put the unique ID field on the axis and the human-readable name in the Tooltips well instead, so the reader still sees the plain-English name on hover without losing the split. On a horizontal bar chart, sort direction affects where a value lands visually: sorting descending by the metric places the best performer at the top and walks the reader down to the worst at the bottom, matching how a reader's eye naturally scans; sorting ascending instead puts the worst performer at the top, which reads as a chart about the leader rather than a chart about the problem that needs attention.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Putting a display-name field on a ranked chart's axis without first checking whether any two entities share that name, silently merging and hiding the true worst or best case. Sorting a horizontal bar chart ascending when the intent is to surface the worst performer, which buries it at the bottom instead of the top. Choosing a chart type (e.g. a vertical column chart) that makes long ID labels unreadable, without noticing and correcting it. Omitting the human-readable name entirely once the ID is on the axis, leaving the chart hard to interpret at a glance.
example_code_for_ai:
# Ranked bar chart configuration:
# Axis  = routes[RouteID]      <- unique, so LAG-07 and APA-01 stay separate
# Value = [On-Time Rate]
# Tooltip = routes[RouteName]  <- human-readable name, without merging bars
# Sort   = On-Time Rate, Descending  <- best at top, worst (LAG-07, 61.4%) at bottom

title: Slicers, Refresh Stamps, and Publishing vs Exporting
learning_objective: Add a slicer that visibly shows its filtered state, add a refresh-stamp measure so a stale dashboard is detectable, and choose between publishing to a workspace and exporting to PDF based on licence availability.
description_for_ai: Every slicer added to a dashboard must visibly show what it is currently filtered to - a dashboard filtered to one value with no visible indicator of which value is a dashboard that gets misread by anyone who did not build it. A refresh-stamp measure such as Last Refreshed = "Data as at " & FORMAT(MAX(dates[DateKey]), "dd MMM yyyy") placed on a visible card exists because a failed data refresh is otherwise invisible: the dashboard keeps showing old data with total apparent confidence, and this one card is the cheapest way to catch that. For sharing the finished report, Publish (File, Publish, select a workspace) requires a Power BI Pro licence and produces a live link the audience can open in a browser without needing Power BI Desktop or the underlying file; without a Pro licence, Publish only reaches 'My workspace' and the realistic fallback is File, Export, PDF, which is static (it will not refresh itself) but is an honest, submittable deliverable.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Adding a slicer without confirming it visibly displays its current selection, leaving readers unable to tell what they are looking at. Omitting a refresh-stamp measure, so a stale or failed refresh goes unnoticed by anyone viewing the report. Claiming or demonstrating a live share-link workflow in a context with no Pro licence, rather than being direct that PDF export is the real deliverable available. Assuming Publish failing silently means a bug, without first checking sign-in status and licence availability.

title: Prompting an AI Assistant for DAX with Full Schema Context
learning_objective: Explain why an underspecified DAX prompt produces a confidently wrong measure, and write a prompt that supplies role, schema, grain, actual column values, and a filter-context correctness requirement.
description_for_ai: A vague prompt such as 'write a DAX measure for on-time rate' can return a measure that looks entirely plausible, passes at the unfiltered total, and then produces a wrong value the moment the report is filtered to a specific slice, because the assistant never saw the actual model, only the words of the prompt. A well-formed prompt instead supplies: a role ('you are a Power BI developer'), the schema (fact and dimension table names), the grain ('one row per delivery'), the actual values found in the relevant column (e.g. Status values are exactly 'On time' and 'Late'), and an explicit constraint that the measure must respond correctly to any filter, including a single narrow slice such as one route. That last constraint is the one most often left out, and it is specifically the requirement that would catch a hardcoded-denominator fault before it ships.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Accepting an AI-written measure because it looks syntactically correct and returns a sensible number at the unfiltered total, without testing it under a filter. Omitting the exact column values (e.g. the literal text of a status field) from the prompt, allowing the assistant to guess spelling or casing. Leaving out the requirement that the measure must respond correctly to any filter, which is the single line most likely to prevent a filter-context fault. Treating a first AI answer as final rather than as a draft to be checked against source data.
example_code_for_ai:
# Weak prompt: "Write a DAX measure for on-time rate."
# Strong prompt: "You are a Power BI developer. I have a star schema.
# Fact: swiftroute_deliveries, 41280 rows, one row per delivery.
# Status values are exactly: On time, Late.
# Dimensions: riders, routes, customers_business, dates (marked date table).
# I need on-time rate to respond correctly to any filter, including a
# single route. Give me the measure, then explain what filter context it assumes."
not_yet_taught: auditing AI-written DAX for specific faults

title: Auditing an AI-Written DAX Measure Against Source Data
learning_objective: Audit a set of AI-written DAX measures by checking each against source data under more than one filter state, and correct a hardcoded-denominator fault and a numerator-equals-denominator fault.
description_for_ai: An AI-written DAX measure must be verified by running it in Power BI against source data at more than one filter state, never accepted on sight. Two specific, real fault patterns to check for: a hardcoded denominator, where a ratio measure divides by a literal number instead of a reference to another measure (e.g. DIVIDE([On-Time Deliveries], 41280) instead of DIVIDE([On-Time Deliveries], [Total Deliveries])) - this reads correctly at the one filter state where the literal number happens to equal the true total, then collapses to a nonsensical value the moment the report is filtered to any subset, because the denominator never moves with the numerator. The fix is to replace the literal number with a reference to the correct base measure. The second fault is a numerator copied into the denominator, so a rate measure divides an expression by an identical copy of itself (e.g. Late Rate = DIVIDE(CALCULATE(...,"Late"), CALCULATE(...,"Late"))), which always returns exactly 100% regardless of the actual data - this fault is easier to catch because it fails the very first prediction check. Correct measures follow the same reference-based CALCULATE/DIVIDE pattern established in Topic 7.3.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Accepting a ratio measure as correct because it returns the right value at the unfiltered total, without also checking it against a filtered subset such as a single route. Missing a hardcoded denominator because the literal number happened to match the true total at the moment of testing. Assuming a measure returning a clean, formatted percentage is automatically meaningful, rather than checking what the numerator and denominator actually reference. Correcting the fault by adjusting the literal number to match the current total instead of replacing it with a measure reference, which reintroduces the same fault the next time the data changes.

title: Four Challenge Moves for Interrogating AI-Generated DAX
learning_objective: Use four specific follow-up prompts to interrogate an AI assistant's DAX output rather than accepting a first answer.
description_for_ai: Four specific follow-up moves turn a one-shot AI request into an actual audit dialogue: (1) 'Explain what filter context this assumes,' which forces the assistant to state its own assumptions explicitly; (2) 'Show me a second way to write this, and the trade-off,' which surfaces alternative patterns and their costs; (3) 'What would make this measure return a wrong number?' which asks the assistant to name its own failure modes before they are discovered in production; and (4) 'I ran it and got five percent, I expected sixty-one, where would you look first?' which turns a discovered discrepancy into a directed debugging conversation rather than a restart. That fourth move specifically converts a one-shot request into dialogue, which is the core discipline being taught.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Treating an AI assistant's first DAX answer as final without applying any of the four challenge moves. Asking only 'is this correct?', which invites a confident yes rather than a specific, checkable explanation. Reporting a discrepancy to the assistant without stating the actual number obtained and the number expected, which prevents it from reasoning about the specific gap. Using the four moves only after a fault is already known, rather than as routine practice on any AI-generated measure.
example_code_for_ai:
# Four challenge prompts, used on any AI-generated DAX measure:
# 1. "Explain what filter context this assumes."
# 2. "Show me a second way to write this, and the trade-off."
# 3. "What would make this measure return a wrong number?"
# 4. "I ran it and got 5%, I expected 61%, where would you look first?"

title: The Named-Decision-Maker Test for a Business Question
learning_objective: Apply the named-decision-maker test to distinguish a genuine business question from a topic, and rewrite a vague topic into a testable question using a fixed sentence template.
description_for_ai: The named-decision-maker test asks: could a specific, named person, in a specific role, at a specific organisation, act differently depending on the answer? If no such person can be pictured, the idea is a topic (e.g. 'analysis of Nigerian fintech transaction data'), not a business question. The fix is a sentence template that forces the missing specifics into the open: named decision maker, type of organisation, what varies, across what dimension, and what they should do about it - assembled into one sentence such as 'For a fraud analyst at a Nigerian fintech, how does the failed-transaction rate vary by bank and time of day, and where should manual review be focused?' The underlying interest can stay the same before and after this rewrite; what changes is that the question now names a person and a decision, which is the entire difference between a topic and a project.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Proposing a topic area ('analysis of X data') and treating it as though it were already a business question. Naming a category of person ('analysts', 'the business') instead of a specific role at a specific organisation when applying the test. Insisting an idea passes the test without being able to state who the decision maker actually is - if the person cannot be pictured, the idea has not passed. Skipping straight to a dataset or method before the question itself has been forced through the sentence template.
example_code_for_ai:
# Weak: "Analysis of Nigerian fintech transaction data." (a topic, not a question)
# Template: [named decision maker] + [org type] + [what varies] +
#           [across what dimension] + [what they should do]
# Result: "For a fraud analyst at a Nigerian fintech, how does the
# failed-transaction rate vary by bank and time of day, and where
# should manual review be focused?"
not_yet_taught: the four sign-off criteria and the too-clean trap

title: The Four Sign-Off Criteria and the Too-Clean Trap
learning_objective: Evaluate a proposed capstone dataset and question against the four sign-off criteria, and recognise the too-clean trap where a proposal can pass all four criteria and still be a weak choice.
description_for_ai: A capstone proposal is checked against four criteria before sign-off: Real (does the dataset come from a genuine, properly licensed source, not fabricated); Sufficient (enough rows and more than one dimension to break the analysis down by); No personal data (no names or identifying columns); and Genuine question (names a decision maker and a measurable difference, verified via the named-decision-maker test). A proposal can pass all four criteria and still be flagged as weak under the too-clean trap: a pre-cleaned, already-scored dataset (e.g. a polished Kaggle competition file) has had its data-quality problems solved by someone else already, and because a significant share of the assessed work is demonstrating cleaning and judgement on messy real data, a spotless file gives the student nothing of that work to show, even though it is a legitimate, real, sufficient dataset with no personal data. The sign-off form itself requires every field to carry a real, honest entry - a genuinely undecided dataset field should be written as a specific, honest statement of what is being considered, not left blank or marked 'TBD'.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Approving a proposal solely because it passes all four listed criteria, without separately checking whether the dataset is suspiciously pre-cleaned. Treating the too-clean trap as a rejection of otherwise valid, real, sufficient, non-personal data, rather than as a caution about how little cleaning work it will demonstrate. Accepting a blank or 'TBD' dataset field on the sign-off form instead of requiring an honest, specific statement of where the search currently stands. Applying the four criteria as a simple yes/no checklist without the deeper judgement of whether the project will demonstrate real skill.
example_code_for_ai:
# Four sign-off criteria, applied to a sample proposal (Kaggle churn dataset):
# Real -> Pass (properly licensed source)
# Sufficient -> Pass (enough rows and dimensions)
# No personal data -> Pass (no names/identifiers in columns)
# Genuine question -> Pass (named decision maker: retention manager)
# Four passes, still flagged: pre-scored competition data has already had
# its cleaning problems solved -> "too clean" trap, weak choice despite passing.
